Hi Product Hunt! 👋 I’m Mateusz, the maker of Secret Key.

The problem: if something happens to you, your family is locked out of everything: email, photos, 2FA codes, crypto, bank. Most password managers offer no real way around that.

What Secret Key does: it protects your password database (e.g. KeePass) and splits the master password into pieces using Shamir’s Secret Sharing. You hand the pieces to people you trust, and you decide how many are needed to unlock it (for example, any 3 of 5). One piece alone reveals nothing.

How access works:

1.   A loved one signs in with their printed card.

2.   They confirm with an SMS code. [...] . Access needs SMS verification and a 48-hour delay you can cancel with one click.

results.title: 10 Digital Legacy Tools to Pass Down Passwords & Files
results.content:
The kit is practical because it is legible and portable. It can live in a safe deposit box, with a passport packet, or with formal estate documents, and it works even if your family is locked out of your phone and cannot pass your device-based authentication steps. 1Password also recommends writing down the Secret Key details needed for sign-in flows, and it notes that administrators can disable Emergency Kits in some business settings, which matters if you’re using a work-managed account.

The executive-level take: 1Password’s kit is strongest when you treat it like a legal instrument. Print it, store it in a controlled location, and ensure the right person has authority and instructions to use it.

## 10. Life After Me [...] ## 9. 1Password Emergency Kit

1Password takes a different route. Instead of “emergency access” as a live feature, it provides an Emergency Kit: a PDF that contains your sign-in address, email, Secret Key, and a place to write your account password. If you store that kit safely, it becomes a controlled offline handoff mechanism for recovery and inheritance planning. [...] That distinction should drive how you assign roles in your family. If you want someone to retrieve a few critical credentials and leave everything else untouched, view-only fits. If you need someone to fully operate the account inventory long-term, takeover can be appropriate, with the understanding that it changes who controls the vault after the waiting period. You can also set the waiting period and the access type per contact so you are not forced into a single all-or-nothing decision.

Bitwarden’s emergency access is also a good tool for “life happens” events that do not involve death, including incapacity and hospitalization. When the only person who knows the master password cannot authenticate, emergency access is the difference between continuity and lockout.

Next, you’ll set up the main account — typically the “admin” or “owner” account. This account will have full access to settings, billing, and user management tools. You’ll also create a strong master password and, in some cases, like with 1Password, a unique Secret Key to access the account securely.

Then, in the password manager itself, you’ll navigate to the user management section to add additional accounts. This is where you’ll invite your family members or your friends if they’re your chosen family. Once they accept, you can assign individual permissions, like read-only access for sensitive information or full access to shared vaults.
